During the late 17th century, Paulista bandeirantes explored the mountains of Minas Gerais in search of precious metals. Between 1693 and 1695, simultaneous gold discoveries marked different regions, including the Rio das Velhas and areas that would become the Ouro Fino region. These gold deposits sparked great interest from the Portuguese Crown and attracted thousands of people seeking wealth.

The Ouro Fino Settlement was officially founded by Guard-major Francisco Martins Lustosa, a Portuguese figure who built the Chapel of Saint Francis of Paula on the site. Initially, the region became the subject of dispute between the Captaincies of São Paulo and Minas Gerais due to the riches found there. It was only in September 1708 that jurisdiction was definitively assigned to Minas Gerais, by order of King João V, following a request from the regent of Minas, Gomes Freire de Andrade.

During the 18th century, Ouro Fino was part of the great economic movement of the Gold Cycle in Minas Gerais. Mining, especially through bateia and canaleta techniques, was the main activity. Portugal imposed heavy taxes, such as the "Fifth" (20% of all extracted gold) and the "Derrama" (complement to reach 1,500 kilos annually to the Crown). Despite initial wealth, gold gradually depleted throughout the century, altering the regional economy.

The transition from the 19th to the 20th century marked the transformation of Ouro Fino. The city evolved from a small mining settlement to a municipality with diversified activities. The textile industry gained increasing importance, consolidating Ouro Fino as part of the Textile Circuit of South Minas. The song "Boy of the Gate" (1955) elevated the city to national awareness, making it a symbol of Mineiro sertanejo culture. Currently, Ouro Fino balances its historical heritage with sustainable development and cultural tourism.
